source_assistant: Answer should state assumptions, a falsifiable hypothesis, measurements, expected confounders, and rollback criteria. Minimum technical points: measure routing distribution, expert capacity overflow, all-to-all time, token dropping/padding, placement, batch composition, and compare routing/capacity policies.
corrected_answer:
Assumptions: the model, expert count, top-k, precision, software build, hardware/topology, request mix, sequence lengths, concurrency, arrival rate, and warm-up are held constant; tail latency means request-level p95/p99. Treat token drops, truncation, and failed requests as quality failures, not merely latency wins. For variant 15, the falsifiable hypothesis is that routing skew or expert-capacity overflow is the dominant cause if a capacity/routing change, at matched offered load, reduces per-expert overflow and p99 while preserving quality and goodput; if p99 remains unchanged after those mechanisms improve, investigate queueing, all-to-all/network, placement, batching, or synchronization instead.

First instrument per-expert token counts, router scores/entropy, top-k assignments, capacity-factor limits, overflow, dropped and padded tokens, queue time, expert compute, dispatch/combine and all-to-all latency, network congestion, placement/topology, batch composition, memory pressure, synchronization, retries, and request outcomes. Stratify by prompt/sequence length, tenant or traffic slice, and concurrency so a hot expert is not mistaken for a global effect. Verify whether skew comes from workload correlation, router behavior, capacity limits, or an implementation/placement defect.

Run a randomized, representative fixed-seed replay and a canary at the same arrival rate. Use matched replicas and change one factor at a time: current policy versus a pre-specified routing/load-balancing or capacity-factor policy, with any extra capacity cost recorded. Report p50/p95/p99 latency, overflow/drop/padding rates, expert imbalance, all-to-all and queue shares, throughput, goodput, cost, and task-quality scores with confidence intervals; inspect slice regressions. Use a held-out workload and disjoint tuning. Confounders include batch-size changes, cache/warm-up effects, sequence-length mix, network contention, kernel/compiler differences, autoscaling, retries, and traffic drift. Do not trade quality or dropped tokens for p99. Restore the prior policy on significant quality/goodput loss, increased drops/errors, SLO regression, instability, or unacceptable cost; preserve traces and configuration for review. Results are provisional and require domain-expert validation.
risks: A routing or capacity change may lower p99 by increasing token drops, retries, padding, or quality failures.
Aggregate metrics can conceal hot-expert, long-sequence, tenant, or traffic-slice regressions.
Replay and canary results may not generalize across workload drift, topology, autoscaling, or software/hardware changes.
evidence_required: Matched randomized replay and held-out evaluation with a configuration and seed manifest.
Per-expert routing, capacity, overflow/drop/padding, queue, compute, all-to-all, network, placement, batch, memory, and request-quality telemetry.
Quality, goodput, SLO, cost, and slice-level confidence intervals before and after the policy change, plus canary and recovery records.
